title: The jewel discourse, alone
tomorrow: if every part of you changes, what's left that's "you"?

cards: The sounds before a long trip: a car door, a last hug, someone at the curb calling, text me when you land. Families have small sounds for keeping each other safe. Buddhist tradition has a chanted one.
Tradition says a city called Vesali was in trouble: drought, hunger, sickness, and spirits roaming the streets. Ananda walked through the city reciting a discourse and sprinkling water.
That discourse is the jewel discourse, and it's still chanted for protection. So what does it ask for?

teach.h: TO EVERY BEING, SEEN OR UNSEEN.
teach.b: It opens by speaking to everyone listening, including the ones you can't see: whatever beings are gathered here, of the earth or of the sky, may all be glad at heart, and listen. Then a surprising request.
Show goodwill to humans, it tells the spirits, who bring you offerings day and night, and guard them.
Then the jewels. Each verse names something precious and true. Whatever treasure there is, in this world or beyond, none equals the Buddha.
The same is said of the teaching, and of the community of noble ones. And each verse lands on the same sound: etena saccena suvatthi hotu.

teach.h: BY THIS TRUTH, MAY THERE BE WELL-BEING.
teach.b: By this truth, may there be well-being. That's the heart of it. The chant doesn't bargain, and it doesn't command.
It sets down something it holds true, and on the strength of that truth, wishes safety. And it wishes widely, to every being gathered, seen or unseen.
At Theravada blessings today, monks may hold a white thread while they chant, and water is sprinkled afterward, the way Ananda's was.
You don't need Pali to feel it. The refrain keeps coming back, like a hand on a shoulder.

how: In Theravada communities monks chant the Ratana Sutta as paritta, protective chanting, at blessings, in times of illness and for new homes; a white thread may be held during the chant and water sprinkled afterward.

o: the Buddha's sermon on giving away wealth to the poor
a list of gems given as offerings at a temple
a chant naming the three jewels, wishing all beings safe

games.q: inside the jewel discourse — tap the pairs.
p: a city in hunger and sickness
how each verse asks for safety

s: the chant mainly asks protection for the people chanting it
it opens to every being gathered, seen or unseen, and even asks the spirits to show goodwill to humans.
each verse ends: by this truth, may there be well-being
etena saccena suvatthi hotu: the refrain that keeps coming back.
the chant praises only the Buddha
it names three jewels: the Buddha, the teaching, and the community of noble ones.

games.q: your little brother is scared of the storm outside. you want to borrow the jewel discourse's way of wishing safety. what do you say?
o: say what's true and steady, then wish everyone safe, him and the dog too
promise nothing bad can happen if he says the right words
tell him the storm isn't really there, so there's nothing to fear
games.why: the chant doesn't promise or command. it names what it holds true, then wishes well-being widely, to every being gathered.

practice: Tap a glass softly with a spoon, or hum one low note, and listen until the sound is completely gone.
Then, on each out-breath, say quietly: may all be safe, sending it to the people you love first and then wider, the way the chant does.

wordCard.voice: The jewel discourse: the Ratana Sutta, a chant naming the three jewels and, on that truth, wishing well-being to every being gathered.

orig.note: Pali: jewel, treasure; the three jewels are the Buddha, the teaching and the community.

carryVoice: Something to keep: may all be safe, said on the strength of what's true. Chant heard.

sources.ref: Commentary to the Ratana Sutta (Vesali, Ananda's recitation)
